02: Geospatial Analytics for Peace

Author

Chia Ka Ying

Published

October 11, 2026

Modified

October 22, 2026

1. Introduction and Study Context

Myanmar has experienced ongoing armed conflict since 1948, following its independence from the United Kingdom. Dominated primarily by ethnic-based struggles for self-determination between various Ethnic Armed Organisations (EAOs) and the national armed forces (the Tatmadaw), the situation entered a critical new phase following the February 2021 military coup. The overthrow of the democratically elected government led by the National League for Democracy triggered widespread civil unrest, which rapidly escalated into nationwide armed resistance.

Today, Myanmar represents one of the world’s most complex and prolonged civil conflicts, characterised by fragmented territorial control, massive civilian displacement and persistent political violence. Conflict is neither spatially random nor static. Peace-building and humanitarian actors need to know where violence clusters, which townships behave unusually relative to their neighbours, and whether clusters are emerging, intensifying or fading.

2. Research Objectives and Questions

2.1 Research Objectives

This exercise uses the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) Project’s records for Myanmar and the MIMU township boundaries to:

  • Aggregate political-violence events to townships and build a township × quarter space-time cube.
  • Use Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA), specifically Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA), to identify spatial clusters (High-High, Low-Low) and outliers (High-Low, Low-High), and Getis-Ord Gi* to identify hot spots and cold spots.
  • Use Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA), which combines time-series Gi* with the Mann-Kendall trend test, to reveal where, how fast and in what pattern armed conflict is evolving.
  • Identify where civilians are most exposed to military air strikes, whether that exposure is tied to front lines, and where the relatively safer areas are, combining the results into a protection map.

2.2 Research Questions

  • RQ1: Where are the statistically significant hot spots and cold spots of armed conflict, and do they differ by type?
  • RQ2: Which townships are spatial outliers, e.g., a violent township surrounded by calm ones?
  • RQ3: Where, how fast and in what pattern has armed conflict evolved between Q1 2021 and Q3 2025?
  • RQ4: Where are civilians most exposed to military air strikes, is that exposure tied to front lines, and where are the relatively safer areas?

2.3 Variables

The analysis uses event counts of armed conflict as the primary variable, measuring how often armed conflict occurs in each township and quarter. Fatalities are introduced only in the value-added analysis, where the objective is civilian protection. There, the number of deaths per event identifies which forms of attack are most lethal to civilians, and this determines the variable analysed in the rest of that section. Fatalities are not used in the LMSA and EHSA because they are highly concentrated in a small number of mass-casualty events, which would let single incidents dominate a township’s results.

Section Analysis Variables Objective
Data wrangling Point map, choropleths, space-time cube conflict_events, battles, remote, vac Map the geographic distribution of conflict
LMSA Local Indicators of Spatial Association conflict_events, battles, remote, vac Hot spots, cold spots and spatial outliers
EHSA Emerging hot spot analysis with Mann-Kendall trend conflict_events, battles, remote, vac Where, how fast and in what pattern violence is evolving
Value-added Lethality check; EHSA; bivariate LISA; protection map fatalities, mil_air, clash Civilian protection and peace-building

4. Data Wrangling

4.1 CRS Transformation

Myanmar spans roughly 92°E–101°E and straddles UTM zones 46N and 47N, so no single UTM zone covers it without distortion. WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647) is used, which contains most townships.

The analysis relies on the fields ST (state/region), DT (district), TS (township name) and TS_PCODE (unique township P-code).

mmr_ts <- mmr_ts_raw %>%
  select(ST, DT, TS, TS_PCODE) %>%
  st_transform(32647)

4.2 Fixing townships and centroids

4.2.1 Multi-part townships

A township may be made of several separate pieces of land, which may lead to two problems:

  • The same township stored as several rows. Every township must be exactly one row, so that it is one location in the space-time cube. We therefore merge rows by TS_PCODE. If each TS_PCODE only has one row, this changes nothing.
  • One row holding many polygon parts. All parts for mapping and assigning events were kept, so events on islands are still counted. But the centroid of a multi-part township can land in a water body or outside the township, which matters for distance-based analysis.
NoteAI Use Disclosure

AI tools were used to draft the R code for reducing the dataframe such that there is only one row for every unique combination of ST, DT, TS and TS_PCODE before performing a spatial union using summarise(), and to find townships with more than one part n_parts. The output was reviewed and run by the author to verify correctness against the study data.

mmr_ts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(TS_PCODE) %>% filter(n > 1) #check for rows that share the same TS_PCODE
[1] TS_PCODE n       
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
mmr_ts <- mmr_ts %>%
  group_by(ST, DT, TS, TS_PCODE) %>% 
  summarise(.groups = "drop") %>%
  st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") %>%
  arrange(TS_PCODE) 
nrow(mmr_ts)
[1] 330
ts_parts <- mmr_ts %>%
  st_cast("POLYGON", warn = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(part_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6) #find the largest piece in kilometres square

ts_parts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(TS_PCODE, name = "n_parts") %>%
  summarise(townships = n(),
            multipart_townships = sum(n_parts > 1),
            total_parts = sum(n_parts),
            max_parts = max(n_parts))
# A tibble: 1 × 4
  townships multipart_townships total_parts max_parts
      <int>               <int>       <int>     <int>
1       330                  41         906       159

Based on the results, there are 41 multi-part townships with 906 pieces in total. The most fragmented township has 159 pieces.

What has been addressed:

  • One row per township: the duplicate check returns no rows, and the merge keeps 330 townships, one row per TS_PCODE. Each township is therefore a single location in the space-time cube.
  • All pieces kept: the merged townships remain multi-polygons, so every island and detached piece is used for mapping and for assigning ACLED events. No events are lost.

4.2.2 Centroids that fall outside boundary

st_centroid is used to compute the geometric center. st_intersects() is used to build a table using ts_centroid and mmr_ts to test TRUE/FALSE for each centroid against the township using sparse = FALSE, while diag() was used to ensure that the comparison is made for each centroid with its own township by comparing the values diagonally down the table.

filter(!centroid_inside) returns a list of centroid that does not fall within the township.

ts_centroid <- st_centroid(st_geometry(mmr_ts))
centroid_inside <- diag(st_intersects(ts_centroid, mmr_ts, sparse = FALSE))

mmr_ts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!centroid_inside) %>% select(ST, DT, TS)
# A tibble: 8 × 3
  ST         DT             TS        
  <chr>      <chr>          <chr>     
1 Kayah      Loikaw         Demoso    
2 Sagaing    Kawlin         Kawlin    
3 Mandalay   Kyaukse        Kyaukse   
4 Rakhine    Sittwe         Rathedaung
5 Rakhine    Kyaukpyu       Kyaukpyu  
6 Yangon     Yangon (South) Cocokyun  
7 Ayeyarwady Labutta        Labutta   
8 Ayeyarwady Pyapon         Pyapon

These eight townships indicated under TS have a centroid outside their own boundary, such as in a water body or in another township. This would impact any distance-based neighbour analysis.

Hence, for each township we take its largest land part and use st_point_on_surface() on that part. The result, which we call the anchor point, will then lie on land inside the township’s main body.

Geometric centroids can fall outside their parent polygon, whereas point-on-surface operations guarantee a point inside it (Lovelace, et al., 2026). For multi-part areal units, Pebesma and Bivand (2023) represent each unit by its largest polygon. This approach combines the two ideas by using a point on the surface of each township’s largest land part.

NoteAI Use Disclosure

AI tools were used to draft the R code that reorders the anchor points to match the township layer using match() on TS_PCODE and the stopifnot() checks that confirm the township codes are in identical order and that every anchor point falls inside the township boundaries. The output was reviewed and run by the author to verify correctness against the study data.

ts_anchor <- ts_parts %>% #build anchor points 
  group_by(TS_PCODE) %>%
  slice_max(part_km2, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% #keep only the largest piece in each township
  ungroup() %>%
  st_point_on_surface() %>% #compute point guaranteed to be inside polygon
  select(TS_PCODE)

ts_anchor <- ts_anchor[match(mmr_ts$TS_PCODE, ts_anchor$TS_PCODE), ]
stopifnot(identical(ts_anchor$TS_PCODE, mmr_ts$TS_PCODE),
          all(diag(st_intersects(ts_anchor, mmr_ts, sparse = FALSE))))

The following plot is used to show the shifting of the original centroid (red) to the anchor point (blue).

off_centroid <- which(!centroid_inside)

anchor_maps <- lapply(off_centroid, function(i) {
  tm_shape(mmr_ts[i, ]) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "grey40") +
    tm_shape(st_sf(geometry = ts_centroid[i])) +
    tm_dots(fill = "red", size = 0.6) +
    tm_shape(ts_anchor[i, ]) +
    tm_dots(fill = "blue", size = 0.6) +
    tm_title(mmr_ts$TS[i], size = 0.9) +
    tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
})
tmap_arrange(anchor_maps, ncol = 4)

The study boundary is then plotted for checking.

tm_shape(mmr_ts) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(ts_anchor) +
  tm_dots(fill = "blue", size = 0.1) +
  tm_title("Anchor points of Myanmar townships",
           position = tm_pos_out("center", "top")) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

Anchor points appear clustered at certain areas, where townships are much smaller. The densely packed anchor points would be taken into consideration when selecting spatial weighing in ection 6.1.

4.2.3 Study Area

After cleaning up the multi-part town and centroid issues, the study area is plotted for visual check.

NoteNote

When the map was first written with older tmap arguments (style = "cat" and palette = "brewer.set3"), tmap 4 converted them automatically. The conversion added a “Missing” category to the legend, even though every township has a state/region value.

The code was therefore rewritten in native tmap 4 syntax: fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical() and fill.legend = tm_legend(). This removes the false “Missing” entry. In addition, the 12-colour Brewer Set3 palette was stretched with colorRampPalette() to give one distinct colour for each of the 18 states/regions. Otherwise colours would repeat and some neighbouring states would share a colour.

mmr_st <- mmr_ts %>% group_by(ST) %>% summarise(.groups = "drop")

n_st   <- n_distinct(mmr_ts$ST)
st_cols <- colorRampPalette(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(12, "Set3"))(n_st)

tm_shape(mmr_ts) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ST",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = st_cols),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "State / Region")) +
  tm_shape(mmr_st) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey20", lwd = 1) +
  tm_title("Myanmar townships by State / Region (n = 330)") +
  tm_compass(position = c("right", "top")) +
  tm_scalebar(position = c("right", "bottom")) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "right")

4.3 ACLED Events

ACLED distinguishes three disorder_types, i.e., Political violence, Demonstrations and Strategic developments. count() is used to compute the occurrence of the ACLED events and kable() is used to generate a table to visualise the variables for further analysis.

acled_raw %>%
  count(disorder_type, event_type, sort = TRUE) %>%
  kable(caption = "ACLED events by disorder and event type") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
ACLED events by disorder and event type
disorder_type event_type n
Political violence Explosions/Remote violence 22925
Political violence Battles 21121
Strategic developments Strategic developments 17833
Demonstrations Protests 14942
Political violence Violence against civilians 9958
Political violence; Demonstrations Protests 261
Demonstrations Riots 45
Political violence Riots 24

After reviewing the data, events whose disorder_type contains “Political violence” were retained for analysis:

  • Battles (armed clashes, territorial changes);
  • Explosions/Remote violence (air/drone strikes, shelling, IEDs);
  • Violence against civilians (attacks, abductions and sexual violence targeting unarmed people).

The following three categories were excluded:

  • Riots coded as political violence (24 events), and the 261 protests coded as “Political violence; Demonstrations” (i.e., protests met with lethal force), which reflect civil unrest rather than armed conflict.
  • Strategic developments (17,833 events), such as arrests, looting and base establishment. These are not violent clashes in themselves and are recorded far less consistently.
  • Demonstrations (14,987 events), comprising protests and riots not coded as political violence. These measure civil resistance rather than armed conflict.
Field Role in this study
disorder_type Violence variable: used to select political violence
event_type Armed-conflict variable: Battles, Explosions/Remote violence, Violence against civilians
sub_event_type Finer breakdown of event_type (e.g. Armed clash, Air/drone strike), used in the value-added analysis
admin1 / admin2 / admin3 State / district / township (used only to cross-check the spatial join)
latitude / longitude Village-level location, used for plotting and for assigning events to townships

4.4 Data Quality Check

acled_raw contains two data-quality fields, geo_precision and time_precision, each coded 1 to 3, where 1 is the most precise. The two fields are independent, where an event can have an exact date but only an approximate location. The interpretation is based on notes.

  • geo_precision: 1 = the exact town or village is known; 2 = only an approximate location is known (e.g. “near” a town, or within a township/district), so the event is placed at the nearest named location; 3 = only the state/region is known, so the event is placed at a point representing that state/region.
  • time_precision: 1 = the exact date is known; 2 = only the week is known; 3 = only the month is known.
acled_raw %>% count(time_precision) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  time_precision     n   pct
           <dbl> <int> <dbl>
1              1 82691  94.9
2              2  4212   4.8
3              3   206   0.2
acled_raw %>% count(geo_precision) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  geo_precision     n   pct
          <dbl> <int> <dbl>
1             1 49261  56.6
2             2 37464  43  
3             3   384   0.4

Events with geo_precision = 3 (about 0.4%) are dropped. Their coordinates mark a state/region rather than the actual location, so assigning them to whichever township contains that point would create artificial hot spots. Events with code 2 are kept, as they are usually located in or next to the correct township. All time_precision codes are kept as the time unit used in subsequent analysis is the quarter of the year.

4.5 Data Filtering

Only conflict events mentioned in Section 4.3 are retained, and events located only to the state/region (geo_precision = 3) are excluded.

This leaves 53,910 events from the original 87,109. Two columns are also added:

  • qtr, the quarter in which each event occurred, used to construct the space-time cube; and
  • modality, which distinguishes air/drone strikes and armed clashes from other forms of violence for the trend charts.
conflict_types <- c("Battles", "Explosions/Remote violence", "Violence against civilians")

acled_ac <- acled_raw %>%
  filter(event_type %in% conflict_types,
         geo_precision < 3) %>%
  mutate(
    qtr      = floor_date(event_date, unit = "quarter"),
    modality = case_when(
      sub_event_type == "Air/drone strike"       ~ "Air/drone strike",
      sub_event_type == "Armed clash"            ~ "Armed clash",
      event_type == "Explosions/Remote violence" ~ "Other remote violence",
      event_type == "Violence against civilians" ~ "Violence against civilians",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

c(raw = nrow(acled_raw), kept = nrow(acled_ac))
  raw  kept 
87109 53910

4.6 Convert to sf object

The latitude and longitude values from the ACLED dataset are used rather than the ACLED’s admin3 text. The township names in admin3 have different spellings, e.g., Hpa-An / Hpaan, which would result in events being accidentally dropped if identified by township names.

acled_sf <- acled_ac %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) %>%
  st_transform(32647)

4.7 Event locations

ACLED records each event at the most precise location available, named in the location field. Where the exact place is known, this may be a village, which sits below the township in Myanmar’s administrative hierarchy. Where only the township is known, the event is placed at the township’s main town. Among events with geo_precision = 1, there are those with location different from their township in admin3, i.e., they are recorded more precisely than the township level (ADM3) on which this study is based. The events are therefore first plotted as points, to show their distribution, before being aggregated to townships for the analysis.

The selected events, except for political violence: riots which makes up just 24 events, are plotted for viewing.

tm_shape(mmr_ts) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey97", col = "grey75", lwd = 0.2) +
  tm_shape(mmr_st) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.6) +
  tm_shape(acled_sf %>% filter(event_type %in% c("Battles", "Explosions/Remote violence",
                                                  "Violence against civilians"))) +
  tm_dots(fill = "event_type",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3")),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE),
          fill_alpha = 0.25, size = 0.05) +
  tm_facets(by = "event_type", nrow = 1, free.coords = FALSE) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, panel.label.bg.color = "white")

4.8 Point-in-polygon join

Events are assigned to townships using st_join to check which township polygon each point falls inside, and attaches that township’s TS_PCODE, TS and ST to the event. left = TRUE keeps events that fall in no township, with empty (NA) township fields, so they can be counted in the next line.

acled_ts <- st_join(acled_sf, mmr_ts %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST),
                    join = st_intersects, left = TRUE)

unmatched <- acled_ts %>% filter(is.na(TS_PCODE))
nrow(unmatched)
[1] 11

Using nrow(unmatched), 11 points were found to fall outside the township polygons. ACLED’s admin3 field, which records the township ACLED attributes each event to, is used to assign these points instead:

  • Events with an admin3 value are matched to values in TS. There were eight of such events.
  • Events with no admin3 value or values that do not match TS values are dropped. There were three of such events.
reassigned <- unmatched %>%
  select(-TS_PCODE, -TS, -ST) %>%
  inner_join(mmr_ts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST),
             by = c("admin3" = "TS"), keep = TRUE)

acled_ts <- bind_rows(acled_ts %>% filter(!is.na(TS_PCODE)), reassigned) %>%
  distinct(event_id_cnty, .keep_all = TRUE)

nrow(reassigned)
[1] 8
nrow(acled_ts)
[1] 53907

This leaves 53,907 events.

4.9 Township-level aggregates

The conflict variables are derived for each township:

Variable Definition
conflict_events All political-violence events
battles ACLED event type Battles
remote Explosions/Remote violence
vac Violence against civilians
clash Sub-event Armed clash (used in the value-added analysis) 
acled_df <- acled_ts %>% st_drop_geometry()

agg_vars <- function(d) {
  d %>% summarise(
    conflict_events  = n(),
    battles    = sum(event_type == "Battles"),
    remote     = sum(event_type == "Explosions/Remote violence"),
    vac        = sum(event_type == "Violence against civilians"),
    clash      = sum(modality == "Armed clash"),
    .groups = "drop")
}

ts_total <- acled_df %>% group_by(TS_PCODE) %>% agg_vars()

# left-join to ALL 330 townships so that zero-event townships are kept
conflict_ts <- mmr_ts %>%
  left_join(ts_total, by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  mutate(across(conflict_events:clash, ~ replace_na(.x, 0)))

summary(st_drop_geometry(conflict_ts)[, c("conflict_events", "battles", "remote", "vac")])

4.10 Space-time cube

4.10.1 Choosing the time bin

The time bin has to suit the process being studied. Armed conflict changes slowly, through offensives, territorial control and campaigns.

As the EHSA applies the Mann-Kendall trend test to each township’s series of Gi* values, one per time slice. At least 8 to 10 measurements are recommended to avoid missing a trend. Quarterly bins would give 19 slices, which is above this minimum.

4.10.2 Building the space-time cube

ACLED records one row per event, so the events are first counted for each township and quarter using agg_vars(). Townships with no events in a quarter would otherwise have no row for that quarter, so complete() adds every missing township–quarter combination and fills its counts with 0. This gives one row for each of the 330 townships in each of the 19 quarters (6,270 rows).

conflict_panel <- acled_df %>%
  group_by(TS_PCODE, qtr) %>% agg_vars() %>%
  complete(TS_PCODE = mmr_ts$TS_PCODE, qtr,
           fill = list(conflict_events = 0, battles = 0, remote = 0, vac = 0, clash = 0))

c(rows = nrow(conflict_panel), expected = nrow(mmr_ts) * n_distinct(conflict_panel$qtr))
    rows expected 
    6270     6270

The space-time cube is built with spacetime(), linking the quarterly counts to the township boundaries through TS_PCODE (location) and qtr (time). is_spacetime_cube() confirms that the cube is complete, with every township present in every quarter.

conflict_stc <- spacetime(conflict_panel, mmr_ts,
                          .loc_col = "TS_PCODE", .time_col = "qtr")
is_spacetime_cube(conflict_stc)
[1] TRUE

5. Exploratory Geovisualisation

5.1 Event distribution across townships

ggplot(st_drop_geometry(conflict_ts), aes(conflict_events)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#3182bd", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Events per township", y = "Townships") +
  theme_minimal()

The distribution is strongly right-skewed. A few townships record hundreds of events while others record almost none. This matters for the choice of spatial weights in subsequent analysis.

5.2 Choropleth maps

To keep the choropleth maps consistent and avoid repeating code, a helper function, map_choro(), is defined once and reused for each map. It classes townships into six quantile groups, as event counts are highly skewed, and overlays state/region boundaries for reference. Only the variable, legend title and colour palette change between maps.

map_choro <- function(sf_obj, var, title, palette = "brewer.reds", n = 6) {
  tm_shape(sf_obj) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = n,
                                                values = palette),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = title, frame = FALSE),
                col = "grey70", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_shape(mmr_st) + tm_borders(col = "grey25", lwd = 0.6) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "right")
}
map_choro(conflict_ts, "conflict_events", "Events") + tm_title("Political-violence events")
NoteAnalysis

Political violence is widespread but highly uneven, ranging from fewer than 15 events in the lightest townships to over 1,000 in the most affected. The heaviest concentration is in the central zone, across Sagaing, Magway and Mandalay, heartland of numerous independently operating resistance forces (Myanmar Outlook: Fighting Is Set to Intensify in the Center of the Country | ACLED, 2026). A second belt of high counts runs down the south-east, through Tanintharyi. Another hot area is observed in Rakhine, where a contested strategic route lies (Myanmar Outlook: Fighting Is Set to Intensify in the Center of the Country | ACLED, 2026). The pattern suggests that violence clusters in contested regions rather than being randomly spread, which will be covered in LISA tests in Section 6.

tmap_arrange(
  map_choro(conflict_ts, "battles", "Battles", "brewer.greens") + tm_title("Battles"),
  map_choro(conflict_ts, "remote", "Explosions/Remote", "brewer.oranges") + tm_title("Explosions / remote violence"),
  map_choro(conflict_ts, "vac", "VAC", "brewer.purples") + tm_title("Violence against civilians"),
  ncol = 3)
NoteAnalysis

The three event types show a concentrate at the central zone, but differ elsewhere. Battles are the most widespread and is noted to have a slightly less concentrated stripe i nthe central zone. Explosions and remote violence, follow a similar pattern but are especially concentrated in the central zone, the south-east and coastal Rakhine. Violence against civilians is the most concentrated, mainly at the central zone with a secondary cluster in the south-east. As each map uses its own quantile classes, colours indicate a township’s rank within that event type and should not be compared directly across maps.

conflict_year <- acled_df %>%
  mutate(year = year(qtr)) %>%
  count(TS_PCODE, year, name = "events") %>%
  complete(TS_PCODE = mmr_ts$TS_PCODE, year = 2021:2025, fill = list(events = 0))

mmr_ts %>% left_join(conflict_year, by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  tm_shape() +
  tm_polygons(fill = "events",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(breaks = c(0, 1, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, Inf),
                                              values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Events"),
              col = "grey80", lwd = 0.1) +
  tm_facets(by = "year", nrow = 1) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, panel.label.bg.color = "white")
NoteAnalysis

Using the same event bins for every year shows how the geography of violence has shifted. In 2021, events were relatively dispersed. From 2022, events intensified and concentrated in the central zone, which remains a core area throughout. In 2023, northern Shan near the Chinese border becomes more prominent, consistent with the launch of Operation 1027 in October 2023. With the collapse of regime forces in northern Shan, other ethnic armed organisations launched syncrhonised attacks across the country (Michaels, 2023). In 2024, events escalates in Rakhine on the west coast and along the south-east through Kayin and Tanintharyi. In 2025, the map appears lighter overall, although this partly reflects the shorter period covered (January to September only). Overall, the conflict has expanded from the central heartland towards the border states rather than receding, which will be covered in EHSA analysis in Section 7.

6. Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA)

6.1 Spatial weights

Comparing the four methods for spatial weights, i.e., polygon contiguity, fixed distance, inverse distance and k-nearest neighbours (KNN), KNN is effective when wanting to ensure a minimum number of neighbours based on geographic proximity and in handling skewed values (as shown in Section 5.1). It is also not sensitive to polygons differing in size, where Myanmar’s township ranges greatly, as with polygon contiguity. The use of KNN ensures that every township has neighbours, including the island townships which are located far from the mainland townships and do not share boundaries. Anchor points are dense in Yangon, Mandalay and Nay Pyi Taw, where urban townships are very small (median about 9 km² in Yangon versus about 1,519 km² nationally). A fixed distance band would give these townships dozens of neighbours and leave large rural townships with very few. The k-nearest-neighbour approach gives every township exactly eight neighbours, regardless of township size.

Four approaches to defining neighbours were considered, i.e., polygon contiguity, fixed distance, inverse distance and k-nearest neighbours (KNN). KNN was chosen for the reasons below:

  • Township sizes vary widely. Contiguity works best when polygons are of similar size, and a fixed distance band would give urban townships dozens of neighbours and rural townships very few. KNN gives every township exactly k neighbours, regardless of size.
  • Every township needs neighbours. Island townships share no boundary with the mainland and would be left without neighbours under contiguity. KNN always finds the k closest townships, so no township is excluded from the analysis.
  • The conflict counts are highly skewed (Section 5.1).

Considering the skewed data, the variables should be evaluated in the context of at least eight neighbours (Modeling Spatial relationships—ArcGIS Pro | Documentation, n.d.). k = 8 will therefore be used for the weight matrix analysis.

nb_knn <- st_knn(ts_anchor, k = 8)
nb_lines <- spdep::nb2lines(nb_knn, coords = st_coordinates(ts_anchor),
                            proj4string = st_crs(mmr_ts)$wkt) %>%
  st_as_sf()

tm_shape(mmr_ts) + tm_borders(col = "grey75", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_shape(nb_lines) + tm_lines(col = "steelblue", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_shape(ts_anchor) + tm_dots(fill = "grey20", size = 0.05) +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE)

The plot shows the linking of eight neighbours to each township, including the island township that does not share a boundary with any other township.

6.2 Weight Schemes

The same k = 8 nearest-neighbour list is used for the weight matrix analysis, with row-standardised weights. Local Moran’s I uses it as is, so each township’s spatial lag is the average of its eight neighbours. Gi* (in the Gi* map and in EHSA) requires each township to be part of its own neighbourhood, so include_self() is added.

Analysis Neighbours Weights Rationale
Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) k = 8 nearest neighbours Row-standardised (W) Spatial lag = average of the eight neighbours
EHSA (Gi* per quarter) k = 8 nearest neighbours including self Row-standardised (W) Gi* includes the focal township (location i) in its own neighbourhood 
conflict_w <- conflict_ts %>%
  mutate(nb = nb_knn,
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)

6.3 Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA)

LISA measures, for each township, how similar its value is to those of its neighbours. It identifies clusters, where a township and its neighbours have similar values, and spatial outliers, where a township differs sharply from its neighbours. This is done by computing the local Moran’s I with local_moran().

Based on the local Moran’s I value, outliers and clusters can be identified:

  • Outlier: Negative if focal township (location i) is associated with relatively low values in surrounding location (location j).
  • Cluster: Positive if focal township (location i) is associated with relatively high values in the surrounding locations (location j).

In either case, the p-value must be small enough for the cluster or outlier to be considered statistically significant. This report uses α = 0.05, as required by the assignment brief.

6.4 Calculating Local Moran’s I

lisa is first created as a function to calculate local Moran’s I value with nsim = 99. This will be used for all armed conflicts and the three event types, i.e., battles, explosions / remote violence, and violence against civilians.

lisa <- function(d, var, nsim = 99) {
  d %>%
    mutate(local_moran = local_moran(.data[[var]], nb, wt, nsim = nsim),
           .before = 1) %>%
    unnest(local_moran)
}

Local Moran’s I is first computed using conflict_events, which looks at total number of armed conflict events per township.

set.seed(267)
lisa_ce <- lisa(conflict_w, "conflict_events")

classify_lisa is a function created to sieve out townships where results are statistically insignificant, i.e., p_ii_sim < 0.05. This ensures that townships are assigned into a quadrant of High-High, Low-Low, Low-High or High-Low, only if the results are statistically significant, where p value is < 0.05.

A Moran scatterplot is plotted to show how the LISA classes arise. Each point is a township, where the x-axis is its standardised number of armed-conflict events, and the y-axis is the spatial lag, the average standardised value of its eight nearest neighbours. The slope of the fitted line equals the global Moran’s I, so an upward slope indicates positive spatial autocorrelation. Townships significant at p < 0.05 are coloured by their LISA class while the rest are shown in grey. The scatterplot complements the LISA mapby showing how strongly each township and its neighbours depart from the mean.

lisa_colours <- c("High-High" = "#d7191c", "Low-Low" = "#2c7bb6",
                  "Low-High"  = "#abd9e9", "High-Low" = "#fdae61",
                  "Not significant" = "grey92")

classify_lisa <- function(l) {
  l %>% mutate(
    lisa_class = if_else(p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(mean), "Not significant"),
    lisa_class = factor(lisa_class, levels = names(lisa_colours)))
}

lisa_ce <- classify_lisa(lisa_ce)
lisa_ce <- lisa_ce %>%
  mutate(z_events     = as.vector(scale(conflict_events)),
         z_lag_events = st_lag(z_events, nb, wt),
         .before = 1)

ggplot(data = lisa_ce,
       aes(x = z_events, y = z_lag_events, color = lisa_class)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = lisa_colours) +
  labs(x = "Standardised armed-conflict events",
       y = "Spatial lag of standardised events",
       color = "LISA (p < 0.05)",
       title = "Moran scatterplot: armed-conflict events") +
  theme_minimal()

The fitted line slopes upward, confirming that armed conflict is positively spatially autocorrelated as townships tend to resemble their neighbours.

lisa_ce %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(sig_p05   = sum(p_ii_sim < 0.05))
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  sig_p05
    <int>
1     104

There are 108 townships that has a statistically significant local Moran’s I value.

6.5 LISA Map for Armed Conflict Events

The function map_lisa() draws the significant classes in colour and greys out non-significant townships, so that only significant results are displayed. State/region boundaries are added for reference.

map_lisa <- function(l, title) {
  tm_shape(l) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "lisa_class",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = lisa_colours, levels.drop = FALSE),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "LISA (p < 0.05)"),
                col = "grey60", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_shape(mmr_st) + tm_borders(col = "grey25", lwd = 0.6) +
    tm_title(title) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "right")
}
map_lisa(lisa_ce, "LISA clusters & outliers: political violence")
NoteAnalysis

The LISA map reveals a strongly polarised conflict geography. The largest High-High cluster forms a block across the central zone. A smaller High-High cluster lies in south. These are townships with high event counts surrounded by similarly affected neighbours, indicating sustained, area-wide conflict rather than isolated incidents.

Low-Low clusters cover the far north, and eastern and southern townships. These are relatively calm townships surrounded by calm neighbours.

Low-High outliers sit on the edges of the conflict zones. They have few events but violent neighbours, making them at risk of spill-over. Only one High-Low outlier appears, confirming that high conflict in Myanmar is rarely isolated. With [n] of 330 townships significant at p < 0.05, the clustering is far beyond what chance alone would produce (about 16 townships).

6.6 LISA by Armed-Conflict Type

The same steps are repeated for each armed-conflict type.

set.seed(267)
lisa_types <- list(
  battles = classify_lisa(lisa(conflict_w, "battles")),
  remote  = classify_lisa(lisa(conflict_w, "remote")),
  vac     = classify_lisa(lisa(conflict_w, "vac")))

The table below summarises the number of townships in each significant class, for all armed-conflict events and for each type.

list(`All armed-conflict events` = lisa_ce,
     Battles = lisa_types$battles,
     `Explosions / remote violence` = lisa_types$remote,
     `Violence against civilians` = lisa_types$vac) %>%
  map_dfr(~ st_drop_geometry(.x) %>% count(lisa_class), .id = "variable") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = lisa_class, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  kable(caption = "Number of townships in each LISA class (p < 0.05)")
Number of townships in each LISA class (p < 0.05)
variable High-High Low-Low Low-High Not significant High-Low
All armed-conflict events 32 68 4 226 0
Battles 33 89 12 196 0
Explosions / remote violence 29 69 6 226 0
Violence against civilians 42 54 6 226 2
  • Battles
  • Explosions / remote violence
  • Violence against civilians
map_lisa(lisa_types$battles, "LISA: Battles")

Battles show the most dispersed High-High pattern (35 townships) of the three event types. Besides the large cluster in the centre of the country, significant High-High clusters appear along the south-eastern coastal strip and north-eastern area near the borders. Ground fighting therefore spans both the central lowlands and several border regions.

Low-Low clusters (87 townships, the most of any type) dominate the Ayeyarwady delta with further clusters in the eastern highlands, where Shan Hills are. These areas record few armed clashes.

Low-High outliers (9 townships) appear mostly in the south, below the coastal High-High cluster. These townships record relatively few battles despite neighbouring active front lines. No significant High-Low outliers are found.

map_lisa(lisa_types$remote, "LISA: Explosions / remote violence")

Explosions and remote violence, which include air/drone strikes and shelling, cluster most strongly in the centre of the country. A second, smaller High-High cluster lies further south-east, inland of the coastal strip. Unlike battles, there is no significant High-High cluster along the south-eastern coast, suggesting that remote attacks there do not cluster in the way ground fighting does.

Low-Low clusters (70 townships) again cover the Ayeyarwady delta and eastern highlands, as well as the far north.

Low-High outliers (4 townships) sit next to the central High-High cluster. These townships record few strikes despite heavily bombed neighbours and could be exposed if the area under attack widens. No significant High-Low outliers are found. The concentration of remote violence in the centre suggests that air and artillery attacks are focused on a core area rather than spread along all front lines.

map_lisa(lisa_types$vac, "LISA: Violence against civilians")

Violence against civilians forms two pronounced High-High clusters (38 townships). The first covers the centre of the country, overlapping the core clusters of battles and remote violence. The second extends along much of the south-eastern coastal strip.

Low-Low clusters (53 townships) appear across the southern delta, the eastern highlands and the far north.

Low-High outliers (4 townships) lie on the edges of both High-High clusters. 2 High-Low outliers appear beside Low-High townships. These may reflect localised targeting, such as arrests or killings, rather than wider armed conflict.

NoteAnalysis

The centre of the country is a significant High-High cluster for all three event types, marking it the core of the armed conflict. Elsewhere the event types differ, i.e., battles cluster in the far north and along border areas, remote violence forms a second cluster in the south-east while violence against civilians is especially concentrated along the south-eastern coastal strip. Low-Low clusters are consistent across types, covering the southern delta and the eastern highlands.

7. Emerging Hot Spot Analysis

7.1 Setting up the space-time cube with custom weights

The k-nearest-neighbour weights, including each township itself, are attached to the cube’s geometry so that EHSA uses them.

conflict_stc_nb <- conflict_stc %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(nb_knn),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1) %>%
  set_nbs("nb") %>%
  set_wts("wt")

7.2 Computing Gi* per quarter

set.seed(267)
gi_stars <- conflict_stc_nb %>%
    group_by(qtr) %>%
    mutate(gi_star = local_gstar_perm(conflict_events, nb, wt, nsim = 99)) %>%
    tidyr::unnest(gi_star)

7.3 Mann-Kendall Test

The Mann-Kendall test checks for a monotonic trend in each township’s Gi* series. It is non-parametric, but it does assume serial independence. Quarterly conflict series are likely to be autocorrelated, so p-values should be read as indicative.

mk_tbl <- gi_stars %>%
  group_by(TS_PCODE) %>%
  summarise(mk = list(unclass(Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)))) %>%
  tidyr::unnest_wider(mk) %>%
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(mmr_ts), by = "TS_PCODE")

mk_tbl %>% arrange(sl, desc(abs(tau))) %>%
  select(ST, TS, tau, sl) %>% head(10) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Townships with the strongest Gi* trends") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Townships with the strongest Gi* trends
ST TS tau sl
Bago (West) Okpho 0.743 0
Bago (West) Minhla 0.719 0
Bago (West) Zigon 0.719 0
Bago (West) Nattalin 0.719 0
Bago (West) Gyobingauk 0.719 0
Bago (West) Letpadan 0.696 0
Magway Chauk 0.696 0
Magway Salin 0.696 0
Mandalay Natogyi 0.696 0
Bago (West) Paukkhaung 0.673 0 
ex <- bind_rows(mk_tbl %>% filter(sl < 0.05) %>% slice_max(tau, n = 2),
                mk_tbl %>% filter(sl < 0.05) %>% slice_min(tau, n = 2))
gi_stars %>%
  filter(TS_PCODE %in% ex$TS_PCODE) %>%
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(mmr_ts) %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS), by = "TS_PCODE") %>%
  ggplot(aes(qtr, gi_star, colour = TS)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96), linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gi*", colour = "Township") + theme_minimal()

7.4 Plotting the EHSA

emerging_hotspot_analysis() combines the per-quarter Gi* significance pattern with the Mann-Kendall trend to assign each township to one of ESRI’s 17 categories. The settings are:

  • threshold = 0.05, to match the assignment’s significance level (the sfdep default is 0.01)
  • k = 1 time-lag neighbour
  • nsim = 99 permutations per time slice
set.seed(267)
ehsa_ce <- emerging_hotspot_analysis(conflict_stc_nb, .var = "conflict_events",
                                     k = 1, nsim = 99, threshold = 0.05,
                                     nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt")
ehsa_levels <- c("persistent hotspot", "intensifying hotspot", "consecutive hotspot",
                 "new hotspot", "sporadic hotspot", "oscillating hotspot",
                 "diminishing hotspot", "historical hotspot",
                 "persistent coldspot", "intensifying coldspot", "consecutive coldspot",
                 "new coldspot", "sporadic coldspot", "oscillating coldspot",
                 "diminishing coldspot", "historical coldspot",
                 "no pattern detected")
ehsa_colours <- c("#67000d", "#cb181d", "#ef3b2c", "#fc9272", "#fdbb84", "#fee0d2",
                  "#d4b9da", "#bcbddc",
                  "#08306b", "#2171b5", "#4292c6", "#9ecae1", "#c6dbef", "#deebf7",
                  "#a1d99b", "#c7e9c0",
                  "grey92")
names(ehsa_colours) <- ehsa_levels

prep_ehsa <- function(ehsa, alpha = 0.05) {
  mmr_ts %>%
    left_join(ehsa, by = c("TS_PCODE" = "location")) %>%
    mutate(classification = str_replace(classification, "oscilating", "oscillating")) %>%
    mutate(class_sig = if_else(p_value < alpha, classification, "no pattern detected"),
           class_sig = factor(class_sig, levels = ehsa_levels))
}
map_ehsa <- function(e, title) {
  tm_shape(e) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "class_sig",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = ehsa_colours, levels.drop = TRUE),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "EHSA (p < 0.05)"),
                col = "grey60", lwd = 0.2) +
    tm_shape(mmr_st) + tm_borders(col = "grey25", lwd = 0.6) +
    tm_title(title) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "right")
}
ehsa_ce_sf <- prep_ehsa(ehsa_ce)
ehsa_ce %>%
  mutate(classification = str_replace(classification, "oscilating", "oscillating"),
         sig = if_else(p_value < 0.05, "p < 0.05", "p ≥ 0.05")) %>%
  count(classification, sig) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(classification, n, sum), fill = sig)) +
  geom_col() + scale_fill_manual(values = c("p < 0.05" = "#cb181d", "p ≥ 0.05" = "grey75")) +
  labs(x = "Townships", y = NULL, fill = "Mann-Kendall") + theme_minimal()

EHSA classifies each township from its quarterly Gi* series (19 quarters) and the Mann-Kendall trend test. Only classes with a significant trend (p < 0.05) are mapped.

Class Meaning
New hot spot Significant hot spot in the final quarter only; never a hot spot before
Consecutive hot spot A single uninterrupted run of hot-spot quarters at the end of the period; never a hot spot before that run; fewer than 90% of quarters hot
Intensifying hot spot Hot spot in at least 90% of quarters, including the last, with significantly increasing intensity
Sporadic hot spot On-and-off hot spot (fewer than 90% of quarters); never a cold spot
Oscillating hot spot Hot spot in the final quarter but a cold spot in an earlier quarter; fewer than 90% of quarters hot
Intensifying cold spot Cold spot in at least 90% of quarters, including the last, with significantly increasing intensity
Consecutive cold spot A single uninterrupted run of cold-spot quarters at the end of the period; never a cold spot before that run; fewer than 90% of quarters cold
Sporadic cold spot On-and-off cold spot (fewer than 90% of quarters); never a hot spot
Oscillating cold spot Cold spot in the final quarter but a hot spot in an earlier quarter; fewer than 90% of quarters cold

Because significance comes from the Mann-Kendall trend test, persistent hot and cold spots, which by definition show no trend, rarely pass the p < 0.05 filter. The absence of persistent hot spots on the maps therefore does not mean that no township is persistently violent.

map_ehsa(ehsa_ce_sf, "EHSA: all political violence")
ehsa_ce_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(class_sig != "no pattern detected") %>%
  group_by(class_sig) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            states = paste(names(sort(table(ST), decreasing = TRUE))[1:min(3, n_distinct(ST))], collapse = ", "),
            example_townships = paste(head(TS, 6), collapse = ", ")) %>%
  kable(caption = "Significant EHSA classes and where they occur") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

7.5 EHSA by Armed-Conflict Events

set.seed(267)
ehsa_types <- list(
  battles = emerging_hotspot_analysis(conflict_stc_nb, .var = "battles", k = 1, nsim = 99,
                                      threshold = 0.05, nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt"),
  remote  = emerging_hotspot_analysis(conflict_stc_nb, .var = "remote", k = 1, nsim = 99,
                                      threshold = 0.05, nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt"),
  vac     = emerging_hotspot_analysis(conflict_stc_nb, .var = "vac", k = 1, nsim = 99,
                                      threshold = 0.05, nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt"))
list(`All armed-conflict events` = ehsa_ce,
     Battles = ehsa_types$battles,
     `Explosions / remote violence` = ehsa_types$remote,
     `Violence against civilians` = ehsa_types$vac) %>%
  map_dfr(~ prep_ehsa(.x) %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(class_sig), .id = "variable") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  kable(caption = "Number of townships in each EHSA class (p < 0.05)")

map_ehsa(prep_ehsa(ehsa_types$battles), "EHSA: Battles")

Hot spots. Battles show only one consecutive hot spot, in the north-central area: a newly sustained front. Sporadic hot spots (19 townships) form a block in the western uplands and smaller pockets in the north and east-centre, pointing to recurring rather than continuous fighting. Oscillating hot spots (22) appear along the southern part of the south-eastern coastal strip, along parts of the western coast and in the far north: areas that were calm earlier but have become active battlegrounds.

Cold spots. Four intensifying cold spots lie around the southern delta’s main urban area, where ground fighting has become ever less likely. Sporadic cold spots (26) cover much of the south-central lowlands, and oscillating cold spots (10) in the north-east have seen battles decline after earlier fighting.

Pattern. Ground fighting is shifting outwards. Its newly emerging hot spots lie at the periphery, in the western uplands, the far north and the southern coastal strip, rather than in the central plains, where LISA shows fighting is concentrated overall.

map_ehsa(prep_ehsa(ehsa_types$remote), "EHSA: Explosions / remote violence")

Hot spots. Remote violence is the only event type with intensifying hot spots (2 townships), in the east-centre. These townships have been hot spots in at least 90% of quarters, and the intensity of air strikes and shelling there is still rising significantly. Three consecutive hot spots and one new hot spot lie inland in the south-east, where remote attacks have become sustained only recently. Sporadic hot spots (7) appear in the far north and north-centre, and oscillating hot spots (17) extend along the southern coastal strip.

Cold spots. Sporadic cold spots (63, the most of any class across the four maps) cover the north-west and parts of the southern delta, with oscillating cold spots (17) scattered in the centre and south.

Pattern. Remote violence shows the clearest signs of escalation of the three event types: it has the only intensifying and new hot spots. These emerging hot spots lie in the east and south-east rather than in the central core identified by LISA, suggesting that air and artillery attacks are expanding to new fronts. The intensifying hot spots warrant particular attention for civilian protection.

map_ehsa(prep_ehsa(ehsa_types$vac), "EHSA: Violence against civilians")

Hot spots. Violence against civilians has no consecutive, intensifying or new hot spots. Its hot spots are only sporadic (22 townships) or oscillating (13), concentrated in the centre-west of the country and in a few south-central townships. Violence against civilians therefore occurs in recurring waves rather than following a steady upward trend.

Cold spots. Ten consecutive cold spots are concentrated around the southern delta’s main urban area, which has seen an uninterrupted run of low violence against civilians in the most recent quarters. Sporadic cold spots (61) run along the western coast and through the central lowlands, and oscillating cold spots (9) are scattered across the centre.

Pattern. The hot spots overlap the central High-High cluster in LISA, confirming the centre as the main area where civilians are targeted. The lack of any intensifying or consecutive hot spots suggests that, while violence against civilians remains concentrated there, it has not been escalating steadily in any one place. The sporadic pattern is consistent with episodic operations rather than continuous campaigns.

Across all event types, EHSA shows the conflict spreading outwards rather than receding. New, consecutive and oscillating hot spots appear at the periphery. The north-central area, the south-eastern interior and the south-eastern coastal strip. Cold spots, by contrast, are entrenched around the southern delta. Remote violence shows the strongest escalation, with the only intensifying and new hot spots, while violence against civilians recurs in waves in the central region. No township is a diminishing or historical hot spot, so there is no statistical evidence of de-escalation anywhere in the study period.

8. Value-Added Analysis: Protecting Civilians from Air Attacks

From late 2023 onward, the military lost territory on the ground and relied increasingly on air and drone strikes.

The chart compares, per quarter, the number of armed clashes with the number of air/drone strikes, split into those by the military and those by other actors. The dashed line marks the launch of Operation 1027 on 27 October 2023, when the Brotherhood Alliance of three ethnic armed organisations launched a coordinated offensive in northern Shan State. Within weeks it captured more than 100 military positions and several towns on the border with China, and it prompted other resistance groups to launch offensives elsewhere. It was the military’s most serious battlefield challenge in at least three decades (Michaels, 2023). The chart shows whether the military’s use of air power changed after this turning point.

acled_df %>%
  filter(modality %in% c("Air/drone strike", "Armed clash")) %>%
  mutate(series = case_when(
    modality == "Armed clash"   ~ "Armed clashes",
    inter1 == "State forces"    ~ "Military air/drone strikes",
    TRUE                        ~ "Other actors' air/drone strikes")) %>%
  count(qtr, series) %>%
  ggplot(aes(qtr, n, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2023-10-01"), linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2023-10-01"), y = 800, hjust = -0.05,
           label = "Operation 1027\n(27 Oct 2023)", size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Armed clashes" = "#1b9e77",
                                 "Military air/drone strikes" = "#d95f02",
                                 "Other actors' air/drone strikes" = "#7570b3")) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%Y-%m") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Events per quarter", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Based on the line chart, armed clashes rose sharply after the 2021 coup, from about 150 in the first quarter of 2021 to over 1,000 per quarter by 2022, and peaked at about 1,600 in the quarter Operation 1027 was launched. Since then, clashes have eased to about 1,100–1,300 per quarter.

Military air/drone strikes followed a different path. They stayed below about 200 per quarter until mid-2023, roughly tripled to about 430 in the quarter of Operation 1027, and then kept rising, reaching about 840 in the second quarter of 2025. Air strikes therefore grew from about one-tenth of the number of armed clashes in 2022 to roughly three-quarters by 2025, even as ground fighting declined.

Other actors’ air/drone strikes grew steadily to a peak of about 340 in early 2024 and have since fallen to about 50 per quarter. The military now carries out most of the air and drone strikes recorded.

Together, the trends suggest a shift in how the conflict is fought: after losing ground from late 2023, the military has relied increasingly on air power rather than ground operations. This sets up the value-added analysis, which examines where these strikes fall and what they mean for civilian protection.
